articles.title: Judge scolds Trump administration after golf course tree removal

paras.en: Oct. 12 (UPI) -- A federal judge on Monday blasted the Trump administration after it chopped down at least 430 trees from a public golf course that President Donald Trump has said he wants to overhaul.
"More than just being upset and furious right now, I am just beyond disappointed with the government," U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said during an emergency hearing.

In May, Reyes told administration officials in court that sufficient notice must be provided before they cut down more than 10 trees or did other maintenance on the course in East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C. The judge is overseeing a lawsuit by the DC Protection League and individuals who seek to block an overhaul of the public course, which Trump has said he wants to convert into a professional facility.

The park has three golf courses. Community activists,including those behind the lawsuit, say the government is illegally redeveloping public land per Trump's wishes. The golf course redevelopment could cost between $20 million and $49 million.
Reyes told government officials that they had lost "credibility" with her, as they gave less than a day's notice before cutting down the trees Sunday.
A Justice Department attorney said they'd done their "best" to give notice, but Reyes replied, "No, you did your absolute worst."
"I trusted you all not to do precisely what you have done," thejudge said.
The DC Protection League asked for the emergency temporary restraining order after the trees were cut down Sunday, saying there was "irreplaceable damage" to the course.
Reyes has barred the National Park Service from cutting down any more trees or doing any further work on the course until at least 2 p.m. Tuesday while she decides about a longer block.

The judge said she had no faith that the government wouldn't continue to cut down trees without a court order. "So now we are all going to have a massive fire drill because the government can't be trusted," she said.

Officials did not give any reasons why the hundreds of trees needed to be chopped down so suddenly, Reyes said. She will require that a top Trump appointee at the Department of the Interior testify about the matter Tuesday.

articles.title: Man dies in fall off roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia

paras.en: Oct. 12 (UPI) -- One person died Monday at Six Flags Over Georgia near Atlanta, police said. Witnesses said the man died in a fall off the Goliath roller coaster.
Cobb County police said several other people were injured in the incident but provided no details Monday.

Aerial video from WXIA-TV of Atlanta showed riders being evacuated from another coaster car that stopped on an incline after the incident. Witnesses told the news outlet that a man was ejected from a car on the ride and hit the ride several times while falling.

"We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today," Six Flags Over Georgia said in a statement. "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends and loved ones. We are also providing support to the guests and team members affected.

"The park team and local authorities responded immediately, and we are cooperating fully with local authorities as they complete their investigation. Out of respect for the family's privacy, we will not be sharing additional details at this time," the statement said.

The Goliath roller coaster opened in 2006 and was manufactured by Bolliger & Mabillard. The park's website called it an "intense70-mile-per-hour thrill ride that challenges even the bravest of the brave."
The incident comes a few weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, Calif., closed its X2 roller coaster permanently after brain injuries and a few deaths were linked to the ride.

"While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it's the right thing to do," park President Brian Oerding said in a statement at the time. "Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously."

articles.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar's home raided in federal criminal investigation

paras.en: Oct. 12 (UPI) -- Federal agents raided Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington home on Monday as part of an ongoing criminal investigation reportedly involving her immigration to the United States.

Federal agents from Homeland Security Investigations descended upon the home of the Minnesota Democrat early Monday morning, Fox News, ABC News and NBC News reported, citing unnamed sources. The outlets said the investigation into Omar stems from her immigration paperwork.

"Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice," a Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement to ABC News. "This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation."

The Justice Department described the investigation as "criminal" but did not disclose the allegations against Omar, who is running for re-election on Nov. 3, as Democrats seek to win a majority in Congress.
Her office confirmed the raid in a statement, calling it "an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."
"For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," her office said.

"Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."

Omar was born in Mogadishu, Somalia, on Oct. 4, 1982, but fled her native country with her family in 1991 during its civil war to a refugee camp in Kenya. In 1995, she immigrated to the United States and was naturalized as a U.S. citizen at the age of 17 in 2000.

The progressive Democrat was first elected to office in November 2016, winning a seat in the Minnesota House of Representatives, the same year Trump won the presidency, and the two have feuded since. Omar has long been a target of Republican criticism, including insults from Trump, who has called her "garbage" and demanded that she be "sent back from where she came from." Critics have characterized some of his remarks as racist.
In a statement from her personal X account, Omar said she was "ok."
"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," she said.
Democrats lashed out at the Trump administration over the raid, which some framed as a direct attack on U.S. democracy.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont who caucuses with the Democrats, called Trump "an authoritarian" who wants to "intimidate his political opponents, the media and all those who disagree with him."
Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., called the raid "fascism and [an] abuse of office on a scale we have never seen."
"This is the stuff of dictatorships," she said in a statement, vowing to "stand firmly" with Omar.

There is no law categorically prohibiting federal law enforcement from investigating candidates close to an election, but the Justice Department has traditionally avoided overt investigative action during that period because of concerns about influencing elections.

The Trump administration has been investigating claims of fraud in state social service programs in Minnesota. President Donald Trump claims that Somali immigrants have been behind widespread fraud in the state.
According to Rep. Jamie Raskin, reporting indicates that the raid concerned alleged fraud involving immigration paperwork her late father filed decades ago when she immigrated to the United States.

Omar is the latest Democrat and perceived political opponent to the president to face federal investigations. Since returning to the White House, Trump has employed the power of the executive office to impose what critics characterize as punitive measures, against targets ranging from law firms linked his critics to sitting lawmakers, including Rep Jason Crow and Sent. Adam Schiff, as well as former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James.

"In none of these cases has the administration succeeded in doing anything other than wasting taxpayer resources and forcing citizens to waste their own precious time and money defending themselves against bogus charges," Raskin, D-Md., ranking member of the House Committee on the Judiciary, said in a statement.

In defense of the raid, the Republican Party of Minnesota quoted Omar as saying in 2023 that American democracy rests on the rule of law and that it is everyone's responsibility to follow the facts where they lead.
"We couldn't agree more, Congresswoman," the Republican Party of Minnesota said in a statement.
"We're sure you still feel the same way now that it's your front door. Minnesotans will be watching closely, and so will we."
Asked about the raid at the White House, Trump told reporters that what he understands is the investigators were "looking at her very carefuly."
"I've always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me," he told reporters.

"I think she's a terrible person, just a complainer. She comes from a country that is a non-country and then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution. I think she's a terrible person, but that's really up to the DOJ."

Border czar Tom Homan, who took over the Trump administration's immigration enforcement operations in Minnesota earlier this year, said last month in a Fox News appearance that Omar was the subject of a Department of Homeland Security investigation.

articles.title: Taylor Swift, Meet The Beatles: How This Dynamic Duo Tells the Story of Now & Then on the Billboard Charts
articles.author: Katie Atkinson

paras.en: This week, Taylor Swift and The Beatles are meeting up on the Billboard charts in more ways than one.

First, both appear in the top 10 of the Billboard 200 albums chart, with Swift’s The Life of a Showgirl spending its 14th week at No. 1 and The Beatles’ deluxe edition of Rubber Soul arriving at No. 4 following its own stint up top in 1966. In addition, Swift’s latest week at No. 1 on the chart means she and The Beatles are the only acts to ever spend 100 weeks in the Billboard 200 top spot (The Beatles have 132 weeks to Swift’s now-100).

On this week’s Billboard Pop Shop Podcast, Katie & Keith are talking about some of the things these two superstar acts have in common across their respective eras and when Swift might reach (or surpass) some big Beatles landmarks, like their record 20 No. 1 hits on the Billboard Hot 100 songs chart.

Also on the show, we’ve got chart news on how the three acts with the most No. 1s on the Billboard 200 — The Beatles, Swift and Drake — are all in the top 10 together for the very first time. Plus, could Tame Impala and JENNIE’s “Dracula” take a bite out of the No. 1 spot on the Hot 100 soon? And, ADÉLA gets her first Hot 100 top 10 with the viral hit “Nicole Kidman.” And we’re also breaking down the big viral news story of the week: Kelly Clarkson’s heated back-and-forth with a Brooklyn art and magic shop.

articles.title: Shakira Closes Historic Madrid Residency With Maluma, Bizarrap & More: ‘Someone Pinch Me’
articles.author: Sigal Ratner-Arias

paras.en: Shakira wanted to end her European residency in Madrid on a high note, and for her 13th concert, she surrounded herself with great friends. Maluma, Laura Pausini, Beéle, Dani Martín and Bizarrap joined her for one last night, which also featured dancers from the Carnival of Barranquilla, a drone display and a visibly emotional Shakira bidding farewell.

“There has been a before and after for me. It’s all felt like a dream, and honestly, I don’t want to leave,” the Colombian superstar told the audience. “It’s going to be very, very hard to leave Spain again.”

Announced a week earlier as “The Last Dance,” Monday’s concert (Oct. 12) brought the residency to a total of 13 shows and concluded with four consecutive performances from Oct. 9-12. The finale also coincided with Spain’s National Day (Día de la Hispanidad), with Latin culture strongly present throughout the celebration.

“I’ve prepared so many, many surprises for you tonight,” Shakira teased shortly after starting the show. “Tonight, I’m not holding anything back. I’m going to give you everything, everything, everything I have, because there’s nothing like when a she-wolf meets her pack.”

The first surprise came with Maluma, who returned for the second night in a row to perform “Chantaje” and “Agua” alongside Shakira. “We’ve already done four songs together; we should form a group called Shaluma,” joked Shakira to her compatriot, who replied that he was ready to create many more songs with her.

Later, Shakira paused the show for several minutes to thank the audience and everyone who made possible what she described as one of “the most important” projects of her career. “This residency has been historic for me,” she said, adding that during these weeks, she had also gone through difficult moments, including her father’s health issues and other personal challenges. She said the audience gave her the strength to step on stage every night “with total joy and a full heart… You’ve made me feel like I’m just starting my career, and I will never forget that.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The superstar then extended her gratitude to everyone who had been part of the show and Macondo Park, as well as Sony Music, Live Nation, her team, musicians and dancers. According to Shakira, more than 10,000 people worked on the production of the show and the themed city that was built around the stadium. She also gave a particularly heartfelt thank-you to her ex Antonio de la Rúa, a current collaborator, introducing him as “a great friend, a soul friend.” Shakira highlighted his support during the tour and his work behind the creation and details of the project.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Following her thank-yous, Laura Pausini took the stage as “the cherry on top,” as Shakira presented her. The Italian artist returned to the residency to perform a duet of “Antología,” as she had during one of the first nights of the residency. Before singing, she took a moment to offer some words, emphasizing what Shakira’s career represents for younger generations of artists. “You are a lesson for so many,” she said. “Just imagine our younger colleagues who see the immense example that you are of a long and very solid career.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The next guest was Dani Martín, former lead singer of El Canto del Loco and one of the most recognized names in Spanish pop-rock, who joined her for “Te Dejo Madrid.” Shakira introduced him with a nod to the song’s lyrics: “Today, I’m going to sing this with a Madrileño who won’t break my heart.”

Beéle later joined her for a performance of “Algo Tú,” while several Carnival of Barranquilla dancers filled the stage, bringing a piece of her hometown’s celebration to a night that coincided with Spain’s National Day. For “Dai Dai,” the Ghetto Kids joined the celebration in a particularly colorful and vibrant evening.

The final performance also highlighted just how far the residency had come. “When they proposed doing eight concerts here in Madrid, I thought it would be impossible,” Shakira shared. “And look, today is our 13th show. Someone pinch me, please, so I know if this is real or not.” According to the artist, around 700,000 people attended the shows at the Shakira Stadium during the entire residency.

The energy remained high throughout the residency, both on stage and among the audience. Purple wigs and chain belts with coins became a recurring sight among attendees, who embraced some of the most iconic images from different stages of Shakira’s career. Near the end of the show, dozens of drones lit up the sky, first forming the shape of a she-wolf and then a giant “12+1,” the chosen way to mark the final night of the residency.

But one last surprise was still in store. Bizarrap took the stage for the grand finale, stepping behind the turntable to perform “Shakira: Bzrp Music Sessions, Vol. 53” with the singer, keeping the party alive until the final moments of “The Last Dance” and bringing nearly a month of Shakira in Madrid to a spectacular close.

articles.title: Maren Morris, Flavor Flav, Maggie Baird & More Speak Out Against Shane Gillis ‘SNL’ Monologue: ‘It’s Actually Dangerous for Women’
articles.author: Katie Atkinson

paras.en: When he returned to host Saturday Night Live for a third time over the weekend, comedian Shane Gillis garnered a lot of attention for his monologue — and the response has been heated. One of the most vocal critics was Schitt’s Creek star Dan Levy, who posted an Instagram video on Sunday to explain why he took issue with the monologue, and to one part in particular.

The joke in question was when Gillis said, “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now? I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. The shorts. Have you seen the shorts?”
In his response video, captioned “Ffs,” Levy said in part, “Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them whores; it makes the men calling them whores misogynists.”

His comments section was flooded with support, including from a handful of music stars. Jewel thanked Levy, while Wicked star Kristin Chenoweth posted a “100” emoji and Lisa Loeb commented alongside a fire emoji “Thank you.”

Maggie Baird, the activist mother of Billie Eilish and FINNEAS, shared Levy’s video to her Instagram Story with her own lengthy caption. “Thank you [Dan Levy]!” she started. “I literally gasped when [Shane Gillis] said this on [SNL]. I felt it physically (and was reminded of the horrible Bill Burr monologue),” she added, referencing Burr’s controversial 2020 appearance on the sketch comedy show, when he complained that white women had hijacked the “woke” movement and that Pride Month shouldn’t be so long. Baird continued: “I come from the sketch comedy world and am not squeamish around comedy, but how can men and comedy writers still think this is funny! It’s actually dangerous for women to promote this bullsh–.”

paras.en: Flavor Flav also platformed Levy’s video, sharing an article about his response on X with the message: “Important allyship.”

Maren Morris added to the discourse in her own Instagram post as well, with the message “me being a wh0re at the gym” across a video of herself soundtracked by her song “be a bitch.” In the video, she throws up a middle finger to the camera and finished it off with the caption: “leave my gym short wedgie out of it.”

Gillis hosted Saturday’s show with Rosalía as the musical guest. In addition to it being his third time hosting, Gillis was also briefly a cast member of the show, but he was dismissed soon after the announcement of his casting when previous homophobic and racist jokes of his resurfaced.

articles.title: EJAE Honored at Gyopo’s Chuseok Benefit: “I’m So Proud to Celebrate Where We Come From”
articles.author: Nicole Fell

paras.en: Singer-songwriter EJAE was honored at Gyopo’s annual Chuseok Benefit.

The KPop Demon Hunters star is fresh off a whirlwind start to the year after the animated film dominated the awards circuit. EJAE earned herself Golden Globe, Grammy Award and an Oscar along the way. The singer was honored at Gyopo’s 8th annual Chuseok Benefit, which is sponsored by CJ ENM, late last month.

“I’m so honored to be recognized by GYOPO at this year’s Chuseok Benefit. It means so much to be surrounded by a community that celebrates the Korean diaspora and the many different ways we stay connected to our culture, because that connection is at the core of what I do,” she told The Hollywood Reporter.
“It’s been such a special afternoon,” she said. “I’m so proud to celebrate where we come from and what we’re creating together.”

The benefit, held Gyopo board member Ann Soh Woods’ private residence, brought together figures from art, design, entertainment and fashion, including Anicka Yi, Carol Lim,, Dumbfoundead, Jon Moon and fellow Demon Hunters stars Audrey Nuna and Kevin Woo. The event is held in early Autumn during the Korean harvest mon holiday Chuseok, which signifies a time to come together.

“We celebrate EJAE’s exhilarating artistic talent and its power to define an era of popular music and culture. EJAE’s journey to becoming a global music icon is one of perseverance and courage — complex, layered, and full of twists and turns,” Gyopo’s executive director Yoon Ju Ellie Lee said about the honoree.

She added, “Her story has resonated with millions across the globe, but it is the way she shares it, with clarity, honesty, humility and meaningfully contextualized within a diasporic Korean experience, that has touched the hearts of us at Gyopo. EJAE has used her platform to speak openly about her process, pressure, rejection and transformation. In times like these, we savor the opportunity to honor a kindred spirit such as EJAE.”

articles.title: Linda Duncombe, Banking Executive and Film Producer, Dies at 55
articles.author: Carly Thomas

paras.en: Linda Duncombe, a longtime banking executive and independent film producer, died on Sunday. She was 55.

The SAG-AFTRA Foundation, where Duncombe served on the board of directors, announced her death on Monday. She reportedly died of complications from a stroke shortly after being diagnosed with stage 2 lung cancer.

“We are devastated by the sudden loss of our dear friend and fellow Board member, Linda Duncombe,” Courtney B. Vance, president and chair of the SAG-AFTRA Foundation Board, wrote in a statement. “Linda was an extraordinary leader who brought a wealth of experience, influence and relationships to our Board, but what made her truly special was how generously she shared all of it.

“She believed wholeheartedly in the mission of this Foundation and in the importance of supporting the performers who bring stories to life,” Vance continued. “Linda had a remarkable ability to bring people together, open doors and turn her passion for this community into meaningful support for our work. She brought such warmth, wit and enthusiasm to everything she did. She will be deeply missed by our Board and staff, and by the many people whose lives she touched.”

Born on Feb. 10, 1971, in Australia, Duncombe later graduated from Western Sydney University and Harvard Business School. She then spent more than 35 years in banking, including at Citibank in Australia and later at the company’s subsidiary, Citi Fintech, in New York.

Duncombe moved to Los Angeles in 2019 to serve as the chief marketing, data and digital officer at City National Bank. There, she helped establish business, sponsorship and community relations with organizations such as SAG-AFTRA Foundation, the Recording Academy, the Motion Picture Television Fund and Tribeca Film Festival. She also led City National Bank’s efforts to deliver more than $1.8 billion in PPP loans to support the entertainment industry.

In 2022, she joined the SAG-AFTRA Foundation’s board of directors, where she “regularly attended Board meetings and educational programs, engaged with staff and fellow Board members, and drew upon her extensive relationships throughout the entertainment and business communities to raise awareness and critical support for the Foundation’s mission,” according to the organization.

Duncombe also joined the board of directors for EnCorps in 2025, a nonprofit organization founded by Sherry Lansing that focused on connecting STEM professionals with under-resourced public school students. She specifically worked on the EnCorps STEM Teachers Program.
As for her work as a producer, she worked on the films The Queen’s Jewels, Killing Time and Best Pancakes in the County.

articles.title: Keri Russell Recalls “Having Sex All the Time” With Matthew Rhys on ‘The Americans’ Set
articles.author: Carly Thomas

paras.en: Keri Russell and Matthew Rhys were having their own kind of fun while on the set of The Americans.

During a recent episode of the Dear Chelsea podcast, Russell told host Chelsea Handler that she and Rhys were “having sex all the time,” even while in the characters’ disguises on set. The couple met while filming the FX period spy drama, which ran for six seasons from 2013 to 2018.

“We were falling in love and staying up all night and having sex all the time and just wearing disguises, like, I’m fucking [in] crazy wigs and wearing pearls,” The Diplomat star confessed. “When have you ever worn pearls and [been] fucking in trailers and fucking everywhere. I mean, it was insanity. It was so fun and sneaky, and sexy, and so good.”

The Americans, created by Joseph Weisberg, followed Philip Jennings (Rhys) and Elizabeth Jennings (Russell), two deep-cover KGB spies, who pose as a married American couple running a travel agency in Washington, D.C., during the 1980s Cold War.
After several years of dating, Russell and Rhys welcomed their son Sam in 2016. Russell also shares two children, son River and daughter Willa Lou, with her ex-husband, Shane Deary.

Elsewhere on the podcast, the Felicity actress addressed Rhys not thanking her during his acceptance speeches at the 2026 Emmys for best actor in a comedy series and limited series for his roles in Widow’s Bay and The Beast in Me. Before the ceremony, she recalled telling him, “Take me off your plate. You don’t have to thank me; I know you love me, take me off your plate,” as Rhys was noticeably stressed about the speeches.

articles.title: Global economy to slow less than expected in 2026 as AI boom offsets war hit: IMF

paras.en: BANGKOK — The International Monetary Fund has raised its forecast for global economic growth this year as the AI-driven investment boom helps offset some of the impact from surging energy costs.
The IMF expects the global economy to grow at 3.1% in 2026, up from the 3% projected in July, but slower than the 3.5% rate last year. For 2027, it kept the forecast unchanged at 3.4%.

The UN agency expects inflation at 4.1% in 2027, above the 3.9% it projected in July – when it estimated the Strait of Hormuz would reopen by mid-July, with conditions broadly returning to pre-war levels by March 2027. For the current year, it maintained its 4.7% outlook.

The IMF now estimates that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March next year and return to pre-war state by October. Gulf crude exports averaged 88% of pre-conflict levels in September as traffic picked up, the international body said.

The report was released at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, where finance ministers and central bank governors from the fund's 191 members are meeting to discuss geopolitical tensions, mounting public debt and artificial intelligence.

AI-related investment gave the global economy a "demand impulse" that helped activity in the first half of the year hold up better than expected, despite the Middle East war and trade tensions, the IMF said. Financial markets also stayed largely calm, which the fund said may partly reflect "AI-related exuberance."

For now, "use of buffers and adaptability have helped economies weather the negative shocks," the IMF said, citing measures such as diversifying fuel sources, tapping strategic reserves that have contained the energy-market turmoil unleashed by the Middle East war.

But that cushion is "rapidly narrowing" in the near term, it said. Global oil reserves are being drawn down by about 2.7 million barrels a day, nearing levels that could trigger sharp price moves, and energy constraints could impair the AI-led momentum. The growing unease over governments' fiscal health also adds to the headwinds.
Overall growth is also becoming increasingly uneven. Thirty-two economies now account for 95% of global growth, down from 54 in April.

Countries that have limited exposure to the war-led supply shock and are catering to the AI-led demand are holding up or strengthening. Taiwan is forecast to grow 10.7% this year and South Korea 3.3%, up from 1.1% in 2025 on semiconductor demand. The U.S. is projected to expand 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, supported by private consumption, fiscal policy and tech investment.

Energy importers outside that tech supply chain face higher import bills, weaker real incomes and less fiscal room. The euro zone is estimated to eke out just 1.1% growth this year amid higher energy costs and weak consumer confidence. The Middle East and Central Asia is projected to contract 0.3% this year, with Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar facing double-digit declines before double-digit rebounds in 2027.

China is forecast to grow 4.5% this year and 4.0% in 2027, with higher oil prices and structural headwinds weighing on activity. Second-quarter growth of 4.3% was weaker than expected as sluggish consumption and property strains outweighed robust exports.

"The global economy is not simply slowing or accelerating; rather, growth is being reallocated across countries according to their exposure to the war-induced supply shock and AI-related demand strength," the IMF said.
While AI has underpinned resilience, the investment boom is also adding to inflationary pressures and financial fragility, the IMF said.

"This is a large, front-loaded demand shock" that sees massive investment pouring into sectors such as semiconductors, data centers, and power generation, before any broad productivity gains have materialized, it said in the report.

A potential reassessment of AI-related profitability and productivity prospects could see excessive investment pull back and force a sharp correction in equities. The IMF warned that in a scenario where AI productivity gains fail to materialize, U.S. equities could fall 20% and global growth could end up 1.1% below its baseline estimates by 2028, with Asia 1.7% lower.

Advanced-economy benchmark yields have climbed to multidecade highs as resurgent inflation, the expected path of policy rates and fiscal concerns push up borrowing costs, the IMF said. Technology firms borrowing to finance AI investment are adding to the pressure.

Public debt in advanced economies is projected to reach 115% of GDP by 2031, from 108% in 2025. In emerging and developing economies, it is forecast to climb to 84% from 74%. Primary deficits in the largest economies remain substantially larger than before the pandemic, and governments face higher real interest rates and shorter debt maturities as defense spending pressures mount.
Rebuilding fiscal space is "increasingly urgent," it said, urging governments to keep support for households facing higher energy and food costs "temporary, targeted, and nondistortionary."
Its models put the probability that global inflation exceeds 5% in 2027 at about 35%, up from 30% in April. Risks remain "tilted to the downside," the fund said.

articles.title: SK Hynix, SoftBank shares plunge as tech stocks in Asia track Wall Street chip sell-off

paras.en: Asian technology stocks fell Tuesday as a sell-off in U.S. semiconductor shares spilled into regional markets, with worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition denting sentiment.

Shares of South Korean chip giant SK Hynix, a leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications, plunged more than 8%, while rival Samsung Electronics shed 6.7% — both hit their lowest levels since August.

In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.8%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares.

Tokyo Electron, a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 6.75%, while Advantest, which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 5.65%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell 4.94%, Disco lost 4.69% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.64%.

The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. U.S. memory chipmaker Micron Technology slid 3.9% as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, which reported progress on a new chip structure.

The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the artificial intelligence boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply.
Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates.

articles.title: Six Flags shares plunge after-hours following report of deadly roller coaster incident

paras.en: Shares of Six Flags Entertainment plunged more than 10% in after-hours trading Monday following reports of a deadly roller coaster incident at one of its amusement parks in Georgia, marking a sharp reversal from gains during the regular session.
The stock had closed 4.5% higher during regular trading before the after-hours sell-off.

One person died and several others were injured in an incident involving the park's 200-foot-tall Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia in Cobb County shortly before 4 p.m. Monday, according to the report, citing local police.
Police did not provide additional details about the incident, the report showed.

Witnesses told a local news station they saw a man fall from the roller coaster and strike the ride several times. Riders were later seen being evacuated from the roller coaster after it stopped near the top of the ride, the report said.

Six Flags said its park staff and local authorities responded immediately to the incident, adding that it was cooperating fully with the investigation, had temporarily closed similar attractions across its parks and would not release further details out of respect for the family's privacy, according to the report.
The company's shares have fallen 22% year to date.

articles.title: Why taking a break from exercise might not mean you need to start from scratch

paras.en: Have you ever taken months off training—maybe due to an injury, a new baby or crushing work deadlines – and come back convinced you were starting from zero?
Research from our team has some good news: At the cellular level, you probably weren’t.
We found that muscle and liver cells store memories fromevery training session in ways that may help improve endurance, control blood sugar levels and even slow weight regain after inactivity.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

For most of the past century, long before fad diets and fancy workout trends took off, exercise was considered one of the most effective lifestyle changes to lower the risk of heart disease, Type 2 diabetes, several cancers and early death for people of all ages. But people typically understood exercise as something whose beneficial effects fade away over time: You use it or lose it.

When you stop training, your maximum oxygen uptake, muscle gains and insulin sensitivity drift back to where they started, often within weeks. Physical activity guidelines are built on this fact, which is why they emphasize consistency above all else.

Consistency, however, is a luxury that roughly 3 in 4 American adults aren’t able to enjoy. People can experience injuries, illness, pregnancy or jobs that limit their time for or ability to exercise. If adaptation really resets, every time you step into the gym would be as if you’ve never been there before. But that scenario doesn’t match what coaches and returning athletes typically describe: In practice, people who have trained before can get fit again faster than those who haven’t undergone similar training.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In recent years, however, scientists have started challenging the concept of “use it or lose it.” New research hints that your cells might keep a record of your training history so all of your gains are not completely lost.
We are exercise physiologists who study how cells remember exercise. Our lab and others have shown that the body is able to store a form of exercise memory across different organs.

To study how this exercise memory works, our team of researchers use an ON-OFF-ON exercise training protocol in mice, which involves an initial four- to eight-week training period, followed by detraining—a period of no exercise—and a second training bout. This method allows us to examine how cells form a memory of exercise, maintain a record of exercise through detraining, and recall memories of prior training when exposed again to exercise.

Using this strategy, our team found that skeletal muscle memory accelerates muscle growth. Compared to mice with no training history, mice who retrained grew bigger muscles, and the individual muscle fibers inside those muscles grew too. Larger muscle fibers meant that the working cells were themselves getting bigger, rather than the surrounding tissue.

Looking more closely at these muscle cells, we found that retrained muscle is better at matching energy production to demand– meaning, the muscles were better at drawing from energy stores when it’s needed most – and this ability persists without further exercise. This memory held even when the mice ate a high-fat diet, suggesting that prior training can still offer benefits even when diet is working against those gains.
Muscle isn’t the only body part that learns from exercise. Working muscle needs fuel, and the liver supplies it during and after training sessions.

My colleagues and I found that liver cells also store exercise memory and uses it to feed muscle more efficiently. In both mice and people who trained, stopped, then trained again, their livers released higher levels of a family of enzymes called carboxylesterases. These enzymes chop up lipids circulating in the blood, delivering fat in a form that muscle can take up and burn as it grows.
Recorded cellular memories of exercise may even be passed down to future generations.

In mice, we found that three to four weeks of maternal and paternal endurance exercise can have a lasting effect on their offspring. Compared to offspring born to sedentary parents, parental exercise granted protection against poor blood sugar levels and excess weight gain for an entire year after birth.

Researchers have hypothesized numerous ways that prenatal exercise may affect offspring. For example, maternal exercise might allow offspring to spend more time developing in the womb or lead parents to producer higher quality milk.
But there remains much to be discovered on how parents influence the health of their children and whether their lifestyle could provide a fitness advantage across generations.

Biology has traditionally granted memory to a short list of cells. Neurons store memory in the connections between them. Immune cells store memory so they can recognize pathogens faster and more strongly the next time they encounter them.

Researchers previously considered all other cells to be memoryless; a cell responds to a signal, then returns to baseline without keeping a record of that interaction. But that assumption is now coming apart.

Skin stem cells can keep a record of inflammation, allowing them to heal a new wound faster months later. Human fat cells keep a record of obesity that persists even after substantial weight loss, which may account for why you gain weight faster when switching back to a high-calorie diet—the so-called yo-yo effect.

We propose that every cell in the body remembers exercise, regardless of how little or how much someone trains. The question is how long these records are stored and whether researchers could prolong or expand each cell’s storage capacity. Better understanding of how cells learn and remember exercise, where they store memories and how those memories are preserved could help improve exercise guidelines for those who cannot exercise for prolonged or consistent periods of time.

To be clear, none of these findings are evidence for skipping the gym; nothing in our data suggests the effects of past training can substitute for present training. But there is hope that the work you put into getting in shape isn’t completely lost over time.
Somewhere, deep in your cells, there is a record waiting to be replayed the next time you lace up your running shoes, pick up a pair of dumbbells or want to fulfill a New Year’s resolution.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

articles.title: This beer-making waste may offer a new stream for cleaner water

paras.en: Scientists still haven’t cracked how to turn water into wine—but they might have figured out how to turn beer into clean water. From the literal ashes of breweries’ by-products, researchers made a charcoal-like substance that clings to bacteria, and they are using it to test a new way of filtering water.

In a recent study, scientists heated up a common waste product from beer making called spent malt rootlets, which are little sprouts that grow from barley during the malting process, to produce biochar, a porous material created from burned organic matter. They found that when they mixed this substance with sand and sent water through it, the biochar was able to remove around five times as much Escherichia coli bacteria as a filtration system that used only sand.

Sending water through sand filtered bacteria like a colander: by physically stopping microbes from moving through. But when the team used a sand mix that was 10 percent biochar, the biochar actively glommed on to slow microbes’ passage.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Groundwater is constantly moving through soil. There it can become contaminated with agricultural waste or fecal matter—potentially infecting any humans who drink it. Adding biochar to certain soils could offer a public health solution and “a sustainable approach for water remediation and the protection of groundwater,” says Ioannis Manariotis, senior author on the study and an environmental engineer at the University of Patras in Greece.

Manariotis and his team have also tested whether waste from olive oil and coffee production can have similar water-purifying effects. Now that the researchers have found the beer by-product can filter out bacteria in laboratory conditions, he says, they plan to test its efficacy under more unpredictable real-life conditions. The results were published in the journal Biochar.

Using brewery waste for water filtration in this way is a “proof of concept,” says Alcina Johnson Sudagar, an independent chemistry researcher who studies other beer-making by-products and was not involved in the study. But the repurposing of by-products from this industry for other applications is already common, she says. Leftover brewery grain is frequently used to make animal feed, and other research suggests beer-making by-products can be used for everything from sunscreen to electricity. The brewing process can have up to 11 steps, and each step produces organic waste materials with different chemical makeups—potentially ideal for different uses.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Sudagar says she hopes Manariotis and his team continue to study biochar. Her most pressing question is whether the material can be used more than once for filtration. If it can trap bacteria only once, it quickly becomes waste again, negating its value as a consistent filtration system or sustainable brewery by-product.

As the global beer industry grows, these new and innovative ways of using the by-products are crucial to sustainability, Sudagar adds. “It’s important to continue because the waste produced will keep increasing, and you would need different applications,” she says. “You cannot just send it to one place and say that we are done with it.”

articles.title: Nobel week: light-controlled brains, particles from outer space and mirror molecules

paras.en: Rachel Feltman: Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup.

Some of the biggest stories in science last week were the announcement of the Nobel Prize awards in Chemistry, Physics, and Physiology or Medicine. So we’re going to focus on those groundbreaking research topics today—with a fun little animal story at the end to send us off, of course.

Let’s start with the prize for physiology or medicine, which was announced last Monday. This year’s award went to Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University, Peter Hegemann at Humboldt University of Berlin, and Georg Nagel at the University of Wurzburg in Germany. They were recognized for their discoveries around light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Optogenetics allows scientists to switch individual brain cells on and off. Because neurons use electrical signals to communicate with one another, scientists realized almost a century ago that they could use electrical stimulation to activate brain cells. Optogenetics combines this idea with genetic engineering to allow for more targeted, less invasive, safer cell stimulation than used to be possible. After genetically modifying neurons to make proteins that react to light, researchers can control those cells with a flash of light instead of an electrode.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Hegemann and Nagel contributed to the field by studying a single-celled alga that swims toward light, which they found had to do with a particular protein that opened up pores in the cell membrane when exposed to light. Deisseroth took those findings and applied them to experiments in living mammals.
We spoke to him about his win last week. Here he is explaining the impact of his discovery:

Karl Deisseroth: You know, once you know what matters for function, you can ask: How can dysfunction be addressed? You know, are there cells that cause dysfunction? Are there cells that can counteract dysfunction in a precise way? And what we're doing now is—and many others as well—is we're seeing: how can we leverage this precision to find new treatments, new medications, new neuromodulator approaches that build on this foundation of causality?

You know, this brings an opportunity that might help me communicate more with the public and to share the excitement of science, how discovery happens, how unlikely things get nurtured and that it takes time and it takes risk but that the outcome can be amazing if we’re willing to take the time and the risk.

Feltman: Last Tuesday saw Francis Halzen from the University of Wisconsin–Madison secure a rare solo award in Physics for the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of extraterrestrial origin. Here to tell us more about his contributions to the field is Joseph Howlett, a senior reporter at Scientific American and our resident physics expert. Tell us about those neutrinos, Joe!

Joseph Howlett: So neutrinos are my personal favorite fundamental particle. Of the 17 that we know about, the neutrinos are the ones we know the least. And that's why they've netted five times the Nobel Prize in Physics now.

The main thing that makes neutrinos different from other particles is that they pass through regular matter almost all the time without interacting. So there's neutrinos coming from space, from faraway black holes where super violent things are happening, like supernova and accretion, and these send out these very high-energy neutrinos. They make it all the way to Earth, but almost all the time they pass right through. We never notice that they're here. They're actually passing through us all the time. Neutrinos from the sun go right through our bodies without interacting.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: It's really hard to build a detector that can catch a neutrino. And Halzen had this super ambitious idea to do so at the South Pole. He spearheaded the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. They chose Antarctica because it's a place with a lot of ice, and ice is great because when a neutrino interacts with ice, the light shines right through. It can go right through the ice like it's not there, all the way to whatever cameras you've buried inside.

So that was Halzen's great idea was that the Earth built this natural detector for us, right? All we have to do is put the cameras there to capture the light. So they bored these mile-deep holes with hot water jets and then lowered these strings of expensive cameras into each of them.

They span like a cubic kilometer of ice. And when a neutrino passes through that ice, usually it goes right through, but very rarely it will interact with one of the water molecules and produce a shower of light. And because the cameras are there, they can capture that light and say where that neutrino came from and how much energy it has.
So for the first time, we're able to see these neutrinos from these very, very faraway galaxies.

And actually, IceCube was the first experiment to see neutrinos from outer space, from outside of our solar system with this super high energy. So we've learned a lot about the universe thanks to this one experiment. It's also heralded this new era that astronomers call multimessenger astronomy. Basically, we've been looking at the sky with telescopes for hundreds of years, right? Measuring the light from faraway galaxies, from stars, X-rays even from black holes. But neutrinos are a whole new thing. They're not light. We're able to see the universe through a different lens. And when you combine this with the light measurements from all the telescopes in space and across the world, and you combine them additionally with gravitational wave detectors, which are another new technology that's won a Nobel Prize recently, now we have these three lenses that together can look at the same faraway objects and teach us all kinds of new things about them.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The thing about the multimessenger era is that it's just beginning. IceCube's only been operating for 16 years, and it's got a lot of life left to live, so we're gonna continue to learn all kinds of new things about the universe thanks to neutrinos, especially combined with these other experiments measuring light and gravitational waves.
Feltman: Thanks for breaking that down for us, Joe.

Last but not least is the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, which this year honored Henri Kagan of Paris-Sud University and Kenso Soai of the Tokyo University of Science for their pioneering research on autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. Try saying that one five times fast!

Many molecules come in two versions that are mirror images of each other. They can’t be superimposed over one another, the same way you couldn’t lay your right and left hands on top of each other and get them to line up. That’s called chirality, which happens to be one of my favorite words. When chemists create chiral molecules in the lab, they typically end up with equal amounts of each version. But that's not ideal, because the proteins in your cells—and in the natural world in general—are made from only one of those mirror images. Kagan and Soai figured out how to create just one of those mirror images at a time.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: We’ll wrap up today’s news roundup with a story about a very, very old tortoise. The oldest tortoise, in fact. And not just the oldest tortoise, but the oldest terrestrial animal known to man. His name? Jonathan.

Giant tortoises are known generally for their long lifespans, but at around 190 years old, Jonathan is at least a century older than seems to be standard for his kind. And yeah, he is definitely that old. Photographs have confirmed that he was fully mature when he was brought to the island of Saint Helena in 1882, which means he had to have been at least 50 at the time.

A study published last week in Science Advances aims to explain how Jonathan is still alive and kicking all these years later. Genetic analysis of the tortoise compared with four of his peers apparently revealed mutations associated with DNA repair, cancer, telomere maintenance, mitochondrial health, insulin regulation, and other pathways associated with aging.

The researchers also took a look at the methylation of Jonathan’s genome. Methylation is when a small chemical tag gets added to DNA, which generally serves to turn a gene off. One sign of aging is a process called methylation entropy, which is where random patterns of methylation start to become more common. In other words, your body gets worse at targeting the right genes to switch off, which makes it more likely that some important protein won’t get made the way it’s supposed to.

In Johnathan’s genome, methylation entropy was unusually low in gene regions associated with mitochondrial function, RNA processing, and genome repair. That could give scientists some clues about what genes to target if they want to increase lifespan for other animals.
Speaking of longevity: We’ll be back on Wednesday to talk about why there’s so much shoddy science in this very buzzy field of research.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great week!

articles.title: A ‘phoenix’ planet was born from the ashes of its dead star
articles.author: Lisa Grossman

paras.en: A dead star’s wreckage may be the birthplace of a new planet.

The existence of second-generation planets was predicted theoretically more than 15 years ago. But this “phoenix” world, if confirmed, would be the first actually spotted, scientists report October 5 in Nature Astronomy.
“A phoenix is reborn from the ashes of its predecessor, and this planet is formed from the ashes of the star,” says astronomer Jamie Williams, of the University of Warwick in Coventry, England.
The finding suggests planetary systems can have a second life even after their stars die.

Before this discovery, this planet formation process has been “more like a hypothesis, more like speculation,” says planetary scientist Zifan Lin of Washington University in St. Louis, who was not involved in the new work. “This is the first time we’ve seen evidence for that process.”

Williams and colleagues found signs of the planet in the atmosphere of a white dwarf called HS 0209+0832. White dwarfs are the small, dense cores left behind after low-mass stars — like our sun — puff up into red giant stars at the end of their lives, ultimately blowing all the outer material away.

These stellar corpses are so dense that most chemical elements sink into their centers, leaving them with pristine atmospheres composed of almost entirely hydrogen and helium. But astronomers have found that between a quarter and half of these stars are “polluted” with elements like silicon and iron, which are found in rock.

These elements probably come from shattered planets that the star devoured as it expanded. “They can be probes into the interiors of planets,” Lin says. Astronomers have also found whole planets that seem to have survived their stars’ demise and still orbit the remaining white dwarf. Ironically, some astronomers think these dead stars could be prime hunting grounds for signs of extraterrestrial life.

HS 0209+0832 was a known weirdo. When the Hubble Space Telescope observed it in 1999, astronomers could tell that the white dwarf contained a mysterious mix of chemicals, but they couldn’t identify them. Since then, there have been more detailed studies of how certain atoms would show up in stellar atmospheres, Williams says.

Reanalyzing those observations showed that the white dwarf contains only trace amounts of silicon and almost no iron, Williams and colleagues found. But it does include a ridiculous amount of niobium. This hard, silvery metal, used in jewelry, rocket systems and superconductors, is rare on Earth and had never been seen in a white dwarf.
“We’ve never observed anything in the universe that’s this niobium-rich before,” Williams says. “We were quite confused at first.”

A clue to how it got there came from the element’s origins. Niobium forms in the slow neutron-capture process, or s-process, which mostly occurs in certain red giant stars as they shed their atmospheres and die. Iron nuclei transform into heavier elements in a series of accretion and decay that can take thousands of years.

Material ejected from a dying star could have coalesced into a new planet full of s-process elements, Williams says. Then the resulting white dwarf could slowly sip on the new planet’s atmosphere, leaving a fresh coat of niobium and other s-process elements on the white dwarf’s face.

To support this idea, the team looked at observations of HS 0209+0832 taken with the TESS space telescope, which hunts exoplanets by observing small changes in the light of their stars as planets orbit. The white dwarf’s brightness changes with a period of about 4.4 days, the team found. That’s too slow to be related to the white dwarf’s own rotation.

But it could be explained by a gas giant planet orbiting very close to the star, about 4 percent the distance from the Earth to the sun or 6 million kilometers. Williams imagines it as a silvery version of Jupiter.
“We’re not really sure, if it’s not a planet, what it is,” he says. “A planet is the most reasonable explanation.”

Our sun will one day meet the same fate as HS 0209+0832’s predecessor. We don’t know enough about second-generation planets yet to say whether our solar system could end up with one after the sun dies, Williams says. “But I think it’s definitely possible.”

articles.title: Scientists may have seen dark matter. If they did, what exactly is it?
articles.author: Emily Conover

paras.en: If a recent hint of dark matter is real, it would rewrite physics. Scientists are already trying to read the outline of that new story’s plot. And that’s reignited interest in certain theories, including a long-beloved but increasingly sidelined concept called supersymmetry.

Dark matter is imperceptibly everywhere, an unidentified type of particle pervading the universe but evident based only on its gravitational effects on galaxies and other cosmic entities. On September 1, scientists with the LUX-ZEPLIN, or LZ, collaboration announced they’d seen a signal in their detector that could have been caused by a single particle of dark matter — though it could still be just a blip caused by known physics processes.

In the weeks since the detection, dozens of papers have been posted on arXiv.org purporting to explain what LZ saw. Much interest has focused on a theorized type of particle called a higgsino. If the idea is correct, it would be big. “If we discover it, it would be the first discovery of supersymmetry,” says theoretical physicist Harikrishnan Ramani of the University of Delaware in Newark.

Supersymmetry proposes that for each known particle, there exists a heavier counterpart called a superpartner. It’s an idea that could solve multiple physics puzzles at once, so it has attracted a devoted following of physicists.

One of these hypothetical superpartners, such as the higgsino, could be dark matter. The higgsino is the superpartner of the Higgs boson — a particle discovered in 2012 that explains the origin of mass. “If you asked people in the year 2000, ‘What’s your favorite dark matter candidate?’ probably a lot of people would already have said the higgsino then,” says theoretical physicist Tracy Slatyer of MIT.

In recent years, supersymmetry’s popularity has waned, as particle colliders failed to find evidence for it. But as an explanation for LZ’s dark matter hint, a higgsino seems plausible — at least at first glance. “It comes pretty close to working,” Slatyer says.

The LZ detector, located at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead, S.D., consists of a large tank of liquid xenon. The detector searches for dark matter speeding through the xenon, crashing into it and sending a xenon atomic nucleus zinging away. That’s expected to be a rare event, since dark matter interacts very weakly with normal matter. In the event LZ found, the nucleus recoiled with particularly high energy. Most types of dark matter would produce low-energy recoils in addition to high-energy ones. But LZ didn’t see any low-energy recoils.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If dark matter were a higgsino, that could explain the absence of low-energy events. The higgsino differs from typical dark matter candidates in that it would have two different masses. A collision would happen only if there’s enough energy to bump the higgsino from the lighter to the heavier mass state. That means lower-energy nuclear recoils wouldn’t happen.

Within a day of LZ’s announcement, several papers on the arXiv put forth the higgsino possibility. “I got pretty excited,” says theoretical physicist Katherine Freese of the University of Texas at Austin, a coauthor of one such paper, which was submitted September 1. “First paper I ever wrote in 24 hours.”

But further investigation made the higgsino explanation seem less plausible. For example, if higgsinos exist, they would interact in the sun and get trapped there due to its gravitational pull. There, according to the concepts of supersymmetry, they would annihilate one another and produce high-energy particles called neutrinos. Those neutrinos should have been observed by a neutrino detector located at the South Pole, called IceCube, Ramani and a colleague reported September 2 at arXiv.org. But no such neutrinos have been seen.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And there’s another potential issue. Slatyer and colleagues noticed a plot in an appendix to LZ’s paper that looks at even higher energies. If LZ saw one higgsino at the energy they reported, they’d expect to see even more at these higher energies, the team reported September 3. But LZ didn’t report anything that looked like dark matter at those energies. The LZ detector wasn’t calibrated for those energies, says LZ spokesperson Rick Gaitskell, a physicist at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “We didn’t make any formal claims about detection or even nondetection in that event region,” Gaitskell wrote in a text message. But, if the data are taken seriously, that makes LZ’s event even more difficult to explain with a higgsino.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Considering all these factors makes the higgsino idea a bit of a stretch. But there’s still a little wiggle room. One possibility is that the higgsino’s mass differs from what theoretical physicists expect it to be, about 1,000 times a proton’s mass. That large mass is chosen to allow higgsinos to explain the amount of dark matter seen in the universe today. So changing it complicates the picture, but could make it align better with what LZ saw.

Additional wiggle room comes from the possible speeds of the dark matter particles in the Milky Way. The particles might reach higher velocities than typically assumed, and that could make the data easier to explain. For a faster higgsino to have shown up in LZ, it would require a larger difference in the two masses of the particle. The resulting bigger energy difference means higgsinos have fewer opportunities to produce neutrinos in the sun, explaining why neutrino experiments haven’t seen those particles.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: By playing around with those factors, it’s still possible to make the higgsino explanation work, Freese says. Higgsinos with around 2,000 times a proton’s mass could do the trick, Freese and a coauthor report in an October 2 arXiv paper. “Big picture: We love [the] higgsino, and what we’re doing now is putting in the details that we think are important,” she says.

But, if it’s not the higgsino, “maybe it’s some other particle with the same basic features,” says theoretical physicist Dan Hooper of the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Such particles wouldn’t be subject to the constraints supersymmetry imposes. For example, if the particles collect in the sun, they wouldn’t necessarily create neutrinos, so it doesn’t matter that IceCube doesn’t see them. Hooper and colleagues investigated the possibilities in a paper submitted September 10 to arXiv.org. And in a September 22 arXiv paper, Hooper and colleagues proposed a version of a different class of dark matter particle that could explain two puzzles in one: LZ’s result and mysterious gamma rays, high-energy light, seen coming from the center of the Milky Way.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Other physicists are looking at entirely different ideas, involving hypothesized types of particles such as dark photons. Meanwhile, scientists are eagerly awaiting new results from LZ, to see if additional data hide similar events.

Other dark matter experiments, such as XENONnT at Gran Sasso National Laboratory in Italy, are also taking a look, combing through their existing data to check for high-energy events. LZ’s result “clearly requires a cross-check,” says XENONnT spokesperson Elena Aprile, a physicist at Columbia University.

Even if the result isn’t a slam-dunk for the higgsino — and even though this might not be dark matter at all — scientists are enjoying exploring the possibilities. “I think it’s wrong to throw tantrums over the fact that it’s not the higgsino the way we want it to be,” Ramani says. “Nature might not give us everything we want in one go.”

articles.title: Remember the ‘caregiving kills’ study? Reality is more nuanced
articles.author: Sujata Gupta

paras.en: When social and affective neuroscientist Naomi Eisenberger’s dad developed dementia, she knew the popular wisdom. Caring for him could shave years off her life. But Eisenberger, of UCLA, was skeptical. Caring for her dad, who died in January, was stressful but also meaningful, she says. “It gave me a lot of joy to bring him some happiness.”

Caregiving kills as an idea first emerged in the scientific literature almost three decades ago. Distressed caregivers were 63 percent more likely to die within four years than non-caregivers, psychiatrists Richard Schulz and Scott Beach reported in 1999 in the Journal of the American Medical Association. The finding has since been cited almost 5,300 times, including almost 300 times in the past two years.

But researchers have largely failed to replicate that finding, with considerable research showing instead that caregiving links with living longer, Eisenberger and colleagues report in September in Biopsychosocial Science and Medicine. Caregiving stress may be softened by humans’ hardwired propensity to help others in need, the researchers suspect.

Silence surrounding caregiving’s positives is probably well-intentioned. In 2025, almost one-quarter of all adults in the United States, some 63 million people, provided care to adults or children with a medical condition or disability, according to a 2025 report by AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Almost 65 percent of caregivers surveyed reported experiencing moderate or high emotional stress and almost half reported financial difficulties. Yet financial and emotional support for caregivers remains limited, the report notes.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Highlighting caregiving’s pros could jeopardize what little help is available, says sociologist and gerontologist Rebecca Utz of the University of Utah in Salt Lake City. “I don’t like to take our foot off the pedal and say that caregiving is so positive because it’s hard, and people need support.”

But painting caregiving as wholly negative, rather than nuanced, erases insight into how caregiving might also protect health, Eisenberger and colleagues argue. Most stressors, such as work-related burnout, link with chronic inflammation. Caregiving is less likely to show that link. Understanding that caregiving paradox could reveal how the body can withstand stress, Eisenberger says.

Moreover, helping a loved one may bring unexpected benefits, Eisenberger says. She cites a 2003 study in The Gerontologist showing that adult children who did not care for a parent with severe disabilities experienced more depression than those who did, though the researchers could not show causation. “I’m not suggesting everyone go out and engage in informal caregiving,” Eisenberger says. “I’m trying to make informal caregiving [feel] a little less scary.”
Caregiving was labeled as life-threatening
In highlighting the need for researchers to take caregiver well-being seriously, the 1999 study was groundbreaking, Eisenberger and colleagues write. But it had design flaws.

Schulz and Beach, both of the University of Pittsburgh, compared mortality rates across a four-year period from over 800 individuals. Roughly half the participants had disabled spouses, with some serving as caregivers and others not; the other half had nondisabled spouses and served as the control. Caregiving spouses filled out self-reports indicating their degree of mental strain.

Over the next four years, 103 participants died. Schulz and Beach zoomed in on mortality rates among one subgroup — spousal caregivers reporting considerable strain. Of those distressed caregivers, 17 percent died during the study period compared with 9 percent of control group members.

But buried in the data was another finding, Eisenberger and colleagues note: Individuals not providing care to their disabled spouses still died at the same rate as caregivers experiencing distress. Individuals with sick and healthy spouses occupy different realities, largely invalidating comparisons between those groups, Eisenberger says. In this case, the findings suggest that having a sick or disabled spouse, and not caregiving status, increases one’s likelihood of dying.
More than 6,000 caregivers were asked to evaluate both the sense of purpose and emotional stress associated with caregiving. Their answers illustrate the role’s emotional duality.

The team is not the first to dispute the idea that caregiving kills. That list includes Schulz himself, who coauthored a 2009 Psychological Science study titled, “Caregiving behavior is associated with decreased mortality risk.” (Neither Schulz nor Beach could be reached for comment.) That study, though, has been cited less than 400 times, with just a couple dozen citations in the past two years.

“I … assumed that the field would have taken notice,” says evolutionary and social psychologist Stephanie Brown, an author on the 2009 paper and a similar 2014 review of caregiving in Social Issues and Policy Review. But “slam pieces on caregiving” remain on prominent display in doctor’s offices and other medical settings, says Brown, of the Renaissance School of Medicine at Stony Brook University in New York.
Caregivers are stressed. Biology may help compensate
More recent research hints at why caregiving, a tremendously stressful undertaking, may not kill.

It’s increasingly accepted that stress can trigger systemic inflammation that then compromises the immune system. In theory, stressed caregivers should be inflamed. They’re not, researchers reported in 2020 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. That study relied on data from more than 30,000 U.S. adults. In surveys taken in the early 2000s and the 2010s, participants indicated their caregiver status, type and intensity of care being given, and experiences of strain. They also provided blood samples.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The scientists zoomed in on roughly 250 people who became regular caregivers and analyzed their blood samples for six inflammation-related biomarkers. Those biomarkers did not go up, on average, when people transitioned to caregiving, the team found. Nor did they go up relative to a matched control group of non-caregivers selected from the larger sample. Those findings held true for even the most stressed caregivers, including spouses caring for a partner with dementia.

How, though, are caregivers largely avoiding inflammation associated with chronic stress? “We don’t really know,” says gerontologist and clinical psychologist William Haley of the University of South Florida in Tampa. “There’s a lot of mysteries here.”

Eisenberger and colleagues theorize that the key to the caregiving paradox may lie in a biological system that evolved among mammals to protect offspring that remain helpless well after birth. That “mammalian caregiving system” seems to encourage caring and tamp down the normal stress response that tells people to flee danger, at least when their baby is involved, Eisenberger says.

Studies primarily in rodents hint at how that caregiving system works, Eisenberger notes. And emerging evidence in humans suggests that this system kicks on even in non-parenting contexts, such as holding onto a partner in pain or giving money to family. In preliminary work, Brown and colleagues even saw signs of it among strangers who bonded during an activity.
Researchers are missing fascinating questions

The contradictory feelings Eisenberger experienced while caring for her dad are common. Caregivers can’t disentangle the advantages of the mammalian caregiving system from the strain of helping. Yet over half of caregivers surveyed by AARP reported that caring for a loved one gave them a sense of purpose.

Ironically, minimizing potential positives to protect caregivers may do more harm than good, researchers say. Caregivers may hear only how awful their next several months or years may be. Others might run from the responsibility and later experience regret.
“What if we tell people that … helping others can be really fulfilling even if it can be stressful, too?” Eisenberger says.

Reticence around caregiving’s benefits has also hampered scientists’ ability to advise people undertaking such a difficult role, Eisenberger and colleagues note. Can feeling compassion for a sick loved one turn on the mammalian caregiving system, or does one have to provide care? What if someone has a fraught relationship with the sick family member? Ultimately, when does the stress of opting out of caregiving outweigh the stress of opting in? Framing caregiving as entirely negative means those questions rarely even get asked.
